--- title: "Responsible Use of AI for Non-Coders: BRC and AI Tools" subtitle: "
Bioinformatics Resource Center - Rockefeller University" author: - "[http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_AI_for_noncoders/](http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_AI_for_noncoders/)" - "[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)" --- ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} # Responsible Use of AI for Non-Coders: BRC and AI Tools ::: ## Overview - [The BRC plugin](#brc-plugin) - [BRC code review](#brc-code-review) - [Working with the BRC](#working-with-the-brc) # The BRC plugin {#brc-plugin background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## The BRC plugin The *Customizing Your LLM* session showed [what the BRC plugin can do](Customizing.html#/brc-mcp){target="_blank"}. Here is what is inside it and how a session with it runs. One install adds two things to Claude Code or Codex: - **A connector (MCP)** to the BRC server: nearly 40 tools for your lab's sequencing data, BRC pipelines and BRC training material. - **Four skills** that tell the agent how the BRC does each job, including the mistakes to avoid. ```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"} /plugin marketplace add RockefellerUniversity/brc-mcp-plugin /plugin install brc-bioinformatics@rockefeller-brc ``` The first time a tool is used, a browser window opens for you to sign in with your BRC account. ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes The plugin repository is private for now: the BRC gives access with an account. Installing the plugin does not give access to data. Every request is checked against the user's lab. The same plugin works in Claude Code and Codex. ::: ::::: ## The four skills {.smaller} Each skill loads when your question matches its description, as in the *Customizing* session. | Skill | What it does | Say something like | |---|---|---| | **brc-rnaseq** | Bulk RNA-seq: QC, differential expression, IGV views, expression across your lab's samples | "Compare EpSC vs SB and show me the top genes" | | **brc-scrna** | Single-cell: load a dataset, clusters, UMAP, violin and dot plots, marker genes | "Plot KRT14 on the UMAP of the skin dataset" | | **brc-pipeline** | Your lab's users, sequencing runs and pipeline jobs; QC across assays; start new pipeline runs | "Which of our libraries from last month failed QC?" | | **brc-docs** | Searches BRC training courses and links to the slide it used | "How does the BRC normalise RNA-seq counts?" | The skills hold what the BRC has learned from running these analyses. For example, a sample name can recur across runs, so the skill pins a sample to its run before using it. ## The tools behind it {.smaller} The agent can only use these tools. It cannot browse the server. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Your lab** - Who you are and which labs you can see - Lab members, sequencing runs, FASTQ files, pipeline jobs - Find samples and their QC **Bulk RNA-seq** - Preview, then run, a differential expression report on the HPC - Read DE results; pull expression for any gene across lab samples - IGV sessions, alone or linked to DE results ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Single-cell** - List and load datasets, cell types and metadata - UMAP, violin and dot plots; marker genes - Read-only SQL over the cell table **Pipelines** - Preview, then submit, a BRC pipeline run (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, CLIP-seq) **Training** - Search BRC course material and cite it ::: :::: ## A session with the plugin {.smaller} | You ask | The agent | You | |---|---|---| | "Which RNA-seq samples from our last run look bad?" | Pulls QC for every library and flags the outliers | Decide which to drop | | "Compare EpSC vs SB, without those two" | **Previews** the comparison: samples, groups, design | **Check it and say go** | | "Go" | Runs DESeq2 on the BRC HPC | Wait for it to finish | | "Top 20 genes up in SB. Any keratins?" | Reads the DE results; uses only values the tool returned | Judge the biology | | "Show the top 5 in IGV" | Builds an IGV session linked to the DE table | Look at the tracks | | "Write this up" | Writes a report of the steps, numbers and plots | Read it before you share it | The steps that use compute (a DE run or a pipeline submission) always **stop for your OK**. ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes This is the arc behind the bulk RNA-seq example report in the Customizing session. Good point to stress: the preview step is where most mistakes are caught (wrong samples, groups the wrong way round). ::: ::::: ## Getting access - **You need a BRC account.** Your access follows your lab, so you see only your lab's data. - **It works in Claude Code and Codex.** You also need Node.js, which the connector uses. - **Start with questions that only read data**, such as QC, existing results or plots. Move on to runs once you trust what you see. - **Bring the results to us.** Statistical and biological judgement is for you and BRC staff, not the agent. Ask for access at **[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)**. # BRC code review {#brc-code-review background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## Why review AI-written code? The worst errors in analysis code are **silent**. The code runs and the result looks plausible, but it is wrong: - a contrast the wrong way round - `voom` run on data that is already logged - raw p-values labelled as adjusted - a join that turns missing values into zeros An AI agent writes code like this as confidently as correct code. A clean run is not a correct result. ## biocritic A BRC tool that looks for silent errors in R and Python analysis code. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR R[("Your code
and data")] --> C["Checks
13 rules, no AI
e.g. Excel-mangled
gene names"] R --> M["Two AI reviewers
different model families
read every file"] M --> D["Documentation check
each claim checked against
the package's own docs"] C --> P["Report
file, lines, why it
matters, the fix"] D --> P ``` - **The models run on a BRC GPU.** Your code is never sent to an outside service. - **Two models from different families** have different blind spots. Findings both raise go to the top. ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes Models: qwen3.8-27B and gemma-4-31B, open-weight, served on one L40S GPU on the Rockefeller HPC. The checks without AI also catch DESeq2 alpha differing from the padj cut-off, the wrong species' mitochondrial prefix, genome build mismatches and filters that remove nothing. The report also lists checks that could not run, so "no findings" isn't mistaken for "checked and clean". ::: ::::: ## What it finds {.smaller} A lab's unpublished R analysis (3,939 lines) had four known errors from a manual review: | Error | Found by AI? | |---|---| | A residual computed as `y - slope*x + intercept` instead of `y - (slope*x + intercept)` | Yes, by both models | | Genes missing at 30 min set to a score of 0 after a join | No (one model saw it, called it a design choice) | | `voom` applied to log-scale scores, not counts | Yes, by one model | | A volcano plot labelled "-log10(p-adj)" that shows raw p-values | No | It also flagged a choice worth questioning: negative scores set to 0 before the test. **Two of four found.** The ones it found would have changed the results, so it was worth running. It still didn't replace the manual review. ## How good is it? | Test | Result | |---|---| | 92 test repositories with 83 planted errors | Catches **75%**; about **7 in 10** findings are real errors | | Code from 10 published papers | Found **3 real errors that change results**; most other findings were minor or false | - **It is a screening tool, not a proof.** It misses errors, and some of what it reports is wrong. - **Read every finding.** Treat it like a colleague's comment: usually useful, sometimes wrong. - **A clean report doesn't mean correct code.** ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes Benchmark: planted errors scored automatically against known answers. Without the data checks, recall is 65%. Published code: findings were graded blind. The 3 real errors were ones that change published results. ::: ::::: ## Rebuild the environment The BRC code-reviewer also writes the **recipe to reproduce your code's software environment**. - It reads the packages your code uses. - It writes a **Dockerfile**, an **Apptainer** recipe and a **conda** environment for them. - It lists the packages you use but **never pinned to a version**, a common reason analyses can't be re-run. A result is only reproducible if someone else can rebuild the software it ran on. ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes This comes from the BRC code-reviewer container (local models, seven review dimensions: accuracy, logic, reproducibility, statistics, data leakage, secrets, documentation). The recipes are written to reports/environment/ next to the review. ::: ::::: ## A review vault that remembers {.smaller} With a **review vault** (a folder of Markdown notes, made to open in [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md){target="_blank"}), reviews build up over time: - **One note per finding**, tracked across runs: *open*, *fixed* or *regressed*. Each report starts with "Since last run: 3 new · 2 fixed · 1 regressed". - **You teach it.** Mark a finding *dismissed* and write why. It isn't reported again, and your reason becomes lab knowledge. - **Your lab's rules.** Put conventions in `conventions/` (for example "set a seed at the top of every script") and every review checks them. - **Methods vs code.** Add your methods section as `methods.md` and it checks that the code does what the paper says. A shared vault (for example a private GitHub repository) lets the whole lab see the same findings and decisions. ::::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} ::: notes Same idea as CLAUDE.md and MEMORY.md in the Query and Context session: write things down once in Markdown and every later session uses them. Dismissed findings are counted in the report header, so nothing disappears silently. ::: ::::: ## Using BRC code review The code review tools are **internal to the BRC** for now. - **Send us your code**, or a GitHub repository, before you publish or share an analysis. We run the review and go through the findings with you. - **Include the data**, or its first lines. Some errors, such as Excel-mangled gene names, only show up in the data. - **Include your methods section** if you have one. Ask at **[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)**. # Working with the BRC {#working-with-the-brc background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## Contact Talk to us when you want to: - get access to the **BRC plugin** - have an AI-assisted analysis **reviewed** - choose a method or set up a **reproducible workflow** - try a new AI tool safely with your data **[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)** · [BRC training courses](https://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/){target="_blank"}
